name: Cryotherapy facial

card.summary: A cold treatment of the face, via cooled tools, ice or a spa device, used to temporarily firm, de-puff and tighten the look of skin.
card.note: Dry ice or prolonged contact can injure skin; cosmetic effects are described as short-lived.

quick.overview:
A cryotherapy facial applies cold to the face, in spas through chilled tools or cold air, and at home with ice or cooled rollers. Practitioners say it reduces puffiness, tightens the look of pores and leaves skin looking firmer for a short time.

Research on cold exposure is mostly about whole-body exercise recovery. A small crossover trial of a cooling face mask in runners looked at endurance rather than skin appearance.[1][2]
quick.how: Spa sessions use cold air or cooled instruments on the face for several minutes. At home, people use ice, cold packs or chilled rollers and combine them with a skincare routine.
quick.risks: Cold injury such as frostbite is the main hazard, especially with liquid nitrogen or dry ice. Whole-body cryotherapy is cautioned for people with cardiovascular disease, cold allergy and some other conditions.[2]

lead: A cryotherapy facial is a beauty treatment that cools the facial skin with cold air, cooled tools or ice. Proponents describe temporary de-puffing, a smoother-looking, tighter skin surface and a refreshed complexion.

Cryotherapy in medicine ranges from ice packs to cryosurgery and whole-body chambers. Its main researched uses are exercise recovery and soreness; facial cosmetic uses are not described in the general medical overview.[2]
One randomised crossover trial tested a facial cooling mask in amateur runners and reported 13 percent longer time to exhaustion with the mask, a performance outcome unrelated to appearance.[1]

chain: Skin looks tighter and less puffy for a short period
angle.text: People use facial cold to reduce morning puffiness and to give a firmer look before events. The effect is described by providers as temporary.

paras: Cold therapy is used locally (ice packs, sprays, cryosurgery) or as whole-body exposure in chambers for a few minutes. Whole-body cryotherapy is promoted for recovery, beauty and health.[2]

Chambers using liquid nitrogen carry risks of frostbite and inert gas asphyxiation. Contraindications listed for whole-body cryotherapy include cardiovascular disease, hypertension, acute infection, seizures and cold allergy, and reviews say adverse events are probably underreported.[2] The FDA has said whole-body cryotherapy lacks evidence and should be researched more.[2]

A 2024 randomised crossover trial in 12 male amateur runners tested a facial cooling mask worn before a treadmill time-to-exhaustion test; time to exhaustion was 13 percent higher with the mask than in the control condition. It examined running performance and perceived exertion, not skin appearance.[1] No studies found on cryotherapy facials for skin appearance.

refs.title: Effects of cryo-facial mask on running performance in amateur middle-distance runners
